1:
A boy of seven is set upon the throne of Judah, and the witnesses read the bare accession-notice as the hinge between a rescued dynasty and a reign that will end in blood. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott observes that the verse coincides almost exactly with 2 Kings 12:1-2, merely omitting the note that the accession fell in the seventh year of Jehu; the king is there called Jehoash, of which Joash is a contraction, as Joram is of Jehoram, and the name most probably means "Iahu is a man," though some would render it "Iahu is fire," comparing Isaiah 33:14.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke does the arithmetic the age invites: since Joash had been hidden six years in the temple and was but seven when he came to the throne, he could have been only one year old when his aunt secreted him from Athaliah's slaughter, as at 2 Chronicles 22:10. Clarke also lays out the whole arc of the reign in advance — the purpose to repair the temple, the liberal contributions of the people, the death of Jehoiada, the lapse into idolatry, the stoning of Zechariah, the Syrian invasion, and the king's murder by his own servants. The reformed John Gill keeps to his brief way, glossing the age and referring the reader to the fuller record in Kings where the same matter stands.

But it is the puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry who sets the moral frame the chapter will fill. This account of Joash's good beginnings, he notes, stands almost word for word as at 2 Kings 12, though the latter part of the chapter, concerning his apostasy, Kings scarcely touches; and Henry draws the rule that what is good in men we should take all occasions to repeat, while what is evil we should mention but sparingly, and no more than is needful. He makes the boy-king a lesson for the young: it is a happy thing, when they are setting out in the world, to be under the direction of those who are wise and good and faithful to them, as Joash was under Jehoiada. Let the young reckon it a blessing, and not a burden, to have those about them who will caution them against evil and quicken them to good; for he that will not be counselled cannot be helped. The witnesses do not divide. Ellicott and Gill secure the text and the name, Clarke the chronology and the outline, Henry the theme — a throne preserved for the covenant's sake, filled by a child whose whole after-course would turn on whose counsel he heeded.
2:
The verdict here is favourable but fenced with a qualifier — Joash "did that which was right in the sight of the LORD all the days of Jehoiada the priest" — and the witnesses fasten on that limiting clause as the seed of the whole tragedy. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott compares the wording with the parallel at 2 Kings 12:2, which reads "all his days, while (or because) Jehoiada the priest instructed him"; the phrase "all his days," he explains, is of course relative to the clause that follows it, and the chronicler has accurately given the meaning. The rightness of Joash was bounded by the life of his tutor: he did well so long as a stronger and holier will directed him, and no longer.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch gather the whole reforming work of these years under one head, pointing the reader for the repair of the temple to the fuller record at 2 Kings 12:5-17, where both the formal divergences and the essential agreement of the two narratives may be traced. For them the years "of Jehoiada" are the bright half of the reign, the restoration of the Jahve-worship that the priest had won back from Athaliah's Baalism.

It is the puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry who draws the sombre lesson the qualifier contains. Men may go far in the external performances of religion, he warns, and keep long to them, merely by the power of their education and the influence of their friends, while yet they have no hearty affection for divine things nor any inward relish of them. Foreign inducements may push men on to that which is good who are not actuated by a living principle of grace in their hearts; and in the outward expressions of devotion it is possible that those who have only the form of godliness may out-strip those who have the power of it. Joash, he observes, would prove more solicitous about the fabric of the temple than about being himself a temple to God — for it is easier to build temples than to be temples to God. The witnesses do not divide. Ellicott fixes the grammar of the qualifier, Keil marks the reforming substance of the good years, Henry reads the warning written into that single word "while." A borrowed goodness that leans wholly on another man's faith is a goodness that will not survive his funeral; and the chapter is about to prove it, when the priest whose piety propped the king up is laid at last in his grave.
3:
"And Jehoiada took for him two wives" — and the witnesses are quick to fix the pronoun, for the "him" is the young king, not the aged priest. The reformed John Gill explains that Jehoiada, himself already married to the king's aunt and now upwards of a hundred years old, did not take these wives for himself but chose them for Joash when he was of an age fit for marriage; and observing what mischief Jehoram's match with Athaliah had wrought in church and state alike, the priest was careful to prevent any such disagreeable and dangerous union. The young king, guided by Jehoiada in all things, was guided in this; and Gill judges the women to have been good, one of them being Jehoaddan, the mother of Amaziah named at 2 Chronicles 25:1, though the name of the other is not preserved.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott notes that this statement is not found in the parallel narrative but was doubtless drawn by the compiler from another source; in its place the older record at 2 Kings 12:3 observes rather that the high places were not taken away, the people still sacrificing and burning incense upon them. The two histories, that is, fill the same slot with different material — the chronicler with the king's marriages, Kings with the surviving high places — and each preserves what the other omits.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry turns the verse into a counsel of prudence. It is especially wise for young people to take advice in their marriages, he says, as Joash did, who left it to his guardian to choose him his wives, because Jezebel and Athaliah had been such plagues to the two kingdoms. Marriage is a turn of life which often proves either the making or the marring of young people, and therefore should be attended to with great care and not left to the heat of youthful fancy. Here Henry finds the young king still at his best, submitting the most personal of choices to godly direction. The witnesses do not divide. Gill fixes the true sense of "for him" and names the one wife Scripture records; Ellicott marks the divergence of the sources and what each keeps; Henry draws the practical wisdom. Between them they show a reign still running in its ordered channel — a king married under counsel, a house being built that will carry the line of David down to Amaziah and beyond — the last quiet scene before the death of the counsellor who held it all together.
4:
With the king now grown and married, the narrative turns to the great work of the reign — "Joash was minded to repair the house of the LORD" — and the witnesses weigh both the resolve and the ruin it addressed. The reformed John Gill sets the timing: it was after his marriage, when he was perhaps twenty or twenty-one years of age, that the purpose took shape in him. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke explains why the house needed repairing at all: during the reigns of Joram and Athaliah the temple of God had been pillaged to enrich the house of Baal, and the whole structure suffered to fall into decay, as the king's own words at v.7 will presently declare.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott attends, as ever, to the Hebrew. "Was minded" is literally "it became with the heart of Joash," the same idiom of a purpose conceived in the heart that meets us at 2 Chronicles 6:8 and 1 Kings 8:18; and "to repair" is perhaps best rendered "to restore." He notes that the chronicler gives the account of the restoration in different language from the parallel, appearing to have paraphrased the record he found in his authority, and that the Levites, prominent here, are not so much as mentioned in the corresponding place in Kings.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry lifts the enterprise into a principle. The repairing of houses of worship, he says, is a good work, which all in their places should promote for the decency and convenience of religious assemblies; and he observes how many a good work would lie undone that now gets done, if there were but a few active men to stir in it and lead the way. Yet Henry keeps the sober undertone the whole chapter carries: it is easier, he reflects, to build temples than to be temples to God, and a man may be zealous for the fabric of religion whose heart is not itself a habitation of the Spirit. The witnesses do not divide. Gill dates the resolve; Clarke names the dilapidation that Athaliah's Baal-worship had caused; Ellicott fixes the idiom of a purpose formed in the heart and the chronicler's Levitical interest; Henry commends the work and quietly warns against resting in it. Between them they show a king at the height of his early promise, setting his heart on the noblest of undertakings — the restoration of the house his grandmother had plundered — the good deed that will be remembered against the dark reversal still to come.
5:
The king now sets the machinery of the collection in motion, gathering priests and Levites and sending them out "to the cities of Judah, to gather of all Israel money to repair the house" — and the witnesses trace both the plan and the delay that stalled it. The reformed John Gill notes simply that Joash called the priests and Levites together to communicate his mind and give them their charge. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke draws out the principle behind the levy: since the temple was the property of the whole nation, and its services performed for the salvation of the whole people, it was fitting that each should come forward to help; this, he observes, is the first instance of such a general collection for building or repairing a house of God, and the phrase "from year to year" shows how great the dilapidation must have been, to require such annual exertions to make it good.

The grammatical-historical witnesses fix the wording and the failure. Keil and Delitzsch lay out the king's charge in full — go out, gather the money, and see that ye hasten the matter — and mark the flat sentence that follows, "Howbeit the Levites hastened it not." Charles Ellicott explains that this command is the chronicler's interpretation of the older provision at Kings, "Let the priests take it to themselves, each from his own acquaintance": the priests and Levites of the several districts were to collect the moneys due to the sanctuary, each in his own neighbourhood. The urgent clause he renders "and, for your part, hasten ye in regard to the matter" — and the Levites' remissness, he adds, agrees exactly with the notice at 2 Kings 12:6 that in the three-and-twentieth year of Joash the priests had still not repaired the breaches of the house.

So the witnesses converge on a first plan that faltered. The design was sound and the cause was national, but the agents were slow: the Levites, charged to press the work, let it drag on for years, and the breaches of the temple gaped unmended while the money trickled in. Clarke fixes the breadth and novelty of the appeal; Gill its occasion; Keil and Ellicott the Hebrew of the charge and the documented delay it met. Between them they set the stage for the king's sharp question in the next verse — the reproof of a young reformer whose zeal has outrun the diligence of the very clergy he trusted to carry it out.
6:
The king summons Jehoiada and puts a pointed question — "Why hast thou not required of the Levites to bring in the collection according to the commandment of Moses?" — and the witnesses linger over both the title given the priest and the nature of the tax he had neglected to press. The reformed John Gill takes "Jehoiada the chief" to mean the high priest, or at least the head of his course, the chief of the priests and Levites concerned in the work and indeed the prime minister of the state. The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley notices, by contrast, that the text does not call him the chief priest or high priest but only "the chief" or "the head," a distinction he might hold on other grounds — by his near relation to the royal family, or as chief of one of the twenty-four priestly families.

On the "collection of Moses" the witnesses part company a little. Adam Clarke, also wesleyan-arminian, identifies it with the poll-tax fixed by Moses — the half-shekel levied on every man from twenty years old and upward, reckoned a ransom for their souls that there might be no plague among them, as at Exodus 30:12-14. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott demurs: "the tax of Moses" is here not the half-shekel poll-tax but a more general designation of the moneys appointed for the sanctuary; and "for the tabernacle of witness" he renders "the tent of the testimony," the tent of the Law, comparing Numbers 9:15. He notes too that in the older account the king's question runs differently — "Why are ye not repairing the breaches of the house?" — followed by the order that the priests receive no more money from their acquaintances but hand it over for the repairs, so that thereafter they took no money from the people and did not repair the house.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry reads the scene as the king outrunning the priest in zeal. Joash is more solicitous and more earnest about the repair of the temple than Jehoiada himself, whom he here reproves for his remissness in the matter; and Henry finds in it a quiet irony — it is easier, he says again, to build temples than to be temples to God. The witnesses do not, in the main, divide. Gill and Wesley weigh the priest's title; Clarke and Ellicott the identity of the Mosaic levy; Henry the reproof itself. Between them they show a young king pressing an aged and honoured servant to do his duty, the reformation stalled by clerical slackness now driven forward by the throne.
7:
The verse names the reason the temple lay in ruins — "the sons of Athaliah, that wicked woman, had broken up the house of God, and bestowed all its dedicated things upon Baalim" — and the witnesses divide chiefly over whose sons are meant. The reformed John Gill, following Kimchi, takes them to be sons of Athaliah by some other man than Jehoram, distinct from Ahaziah and his brethren. The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley reads them rather as Ahaziah and his brethren, before they were carried away captive as at 2 Chronicles 21:17, who did this deed at their mother's instigation; and "broke up," he adds, means both that they broke open the treasuries and that they defaced the very fabric of the house.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott agrees that there is nothing corresponding to this verse in the parallel account, and renders it "for Athaliah, the evildoer — her sons had broken down the house of God." Ahaziah and his elder brothers, and perhaps other kinsmen, he judges to be intended; the young princes thus gratified the queen's hatred of the exclusive worship of Jehovah, and it may be that portions of the temple buildings were pulled down to make room for a temple of Baal, as the destruction of that Baal-house at 2 Kings 11:18 would suggest. The "dedicated things" he takes to be the moneys given for the sanctuary's use, and "did they bestow upon Baalim" he renders "they made into the Baals" — used them, that is, in fashioning idolatrous images and symbols, exactly the expression of Hosea 2:8, "her silver and gold, which they made into Baal," and again at Hosea 8:4.

So the witnesses circle a real disagreement of identity while agreeing entirely on the substance. Whether the culprits were Athaliah's sons by a second marriage or the royal princes of Jehoram's line, the crime was the same: a house consecrated to the LORD stripped and battered, its sacred treasures melted down and turned into the furniture of Baal. The verse supplies the black background against which Joash's zeal shines — the very shrine he now labours to restore had been not merely neglected but violated, plundered by the idolatrous house from which he himself had so narrowly been saved. Gill and Wesley debate the parentage; Ellicott fixes the wording and the archaeology of the outrage; all see in Athaliah's brood the hand that had turned the temple's gold into idols, and left to a later king the long work of undoing it.
8:
The remedy for the Levites' remissness is a new device — "at the king's commandment they made a chest, and set it without at the gate of the house of the LORD" — and the witnesses, though brief, mark how the chronicler and the older record differ in the telling. The reformed John Gill and the wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke both pass the reader to the parallel places in Kings, where the same chest is described; Clarke notes only that the fuller notes belong on 2 Kings 12:9 and its neighbours.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott supplies the difference in detail that marks the two accounts. Here the sentence runs impersonally, "the king said, and they made"; but the older narrative at 2 Kings 12:9 is more original and concrete — "Jehoiada the priest took a chest, and bored a hole in its lid" — ascribing the invention to the priest's own hands. And "set it without," Ellicott explains, means outside the temple proper: the chest stood in the court, just inside the gate, where every worshipper entering to pray must pass it and could drop his offering in.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry, weighing the whole scheme, admires the shrewdness of the expedient. When Joash found the money did not come in as he had hoped by the first method, he tried another way, and that way answered the intention. The throwing of money into a chest through a hole in its lid was a device that had not been used before, and perhaps the very novelty of the thing helped to make it a successful means of raising money; men who would not be dunned by collectors would freely drop their gift into a public box set before their eyes. Wisdom herein, Henry says, is profitable to direct, and an invention to please people's humour may sometimes bring them to their duty. The witnesses do not divide. Gill and Clarke defer to the fuller record; Ellicott fixes the divergence between the impersonal chronicler and the vivid older account, and locates the chest at the very threshold of worship; Henry commends the practical genius that turned a stalled collection into a flowing one. Between them they show reformation advancing by a homely means — a bored box at the temple gate — and the king's patience in trying a second road when the first had failed. The device is small, but it will fill; and the next verses will tell how a whole nation, at last given an easy and cheerful way to give, poured its silver into the mending of the house of God.
9:
A proclamation goes out through Judah and Jerusalem, calling the people to bring in the tax "that Moses the servant of God laid upon Israel in the wilderness" — and the two witnesses at hand read it as both a revival of an ancient duty and a mirror the chronicler holds up to his own age. The reformed John Gill notes only that the proclamation was made by heralds appointed for the purpose, publishing the king's will through the towns of the realm.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott gives the verse its philological weight. "They made a proclamation" is literally "they uttered a voice," or a cry, in Judah — a phrase that occurs here alone in this sense, comparable to Wisdom's crying aloud at Proverbs 1:20. The call "to bring in to the LORD" means to bring into the temple, for the LORD; and "the collection" is again the tax, the impost appointed of old. This verse and the next, Ellicott observes, are peculiar to the chronicle, and they betray the writer's characteristic aim: he is fond of dwelling on the willingness of the people in the good old time to contribute to the cause of religion, doubtless by way of gentle suggestion to his own contemporaries, exactly as he dwells on the freewill offerings for the first temple at 1 Chronicles 29:6. Where the older record at Kings says merely that the priests who kept the threshold put into the chest all the money brought into the house of the LORD, the chronicler turns the moment into a scene of national generosity.

Ellicott adds a small correction of the older versions. The clause rendered "until they had made an end" is right, the same phrase recurring at 2 Chronicles 31:1; the ancient versions that give "until it was filled" have mistaken the verb, which means to finish an action, not to fill a vessel. The two witnesses do not divide. Gill fixes the plain machinery of the herald's cry; Ellicott the idiom, the source, and the didactic purpose behind it. Between them they show the reformation carried to the people at large by open proclamation — the whole nation summoned to a duty their fathers had let lapse — and the chronicler quietly preaching to his readers through the story, that the money once poured out so freely for the house of God might shame a later and colder generation into the like liberality. The stage is set for the great inflow that the next verse records, when princes and people together answer the call with joy.
10:
The appeal is answered with gladness — "all the princes and all the people rejoiced, and brought in, and cast into the chest, until they had made an end" — and the witnesses read the cheerfulness of the giving as the true measure of a good work well contrived. The reformed John Gill marks the spirit of it: when the people heard the proclamation, and understood for what use the money was wanted and in what easy manner it might be given, the whole matter was agreeable and pleasing to them, so that they came with ready hearts to the chest.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry dwells on that rejoicing and draws his lessons from it. A great deal was thrown in, he observes, and thrown in with a great deal of cheerfulness — they all rejoiced — and this is the note the chronicler wishes his reader to catch. Henry finds in the whole episode a pattern of how good works prosper. Many, he says, have honesty enough to follow that have not zeal enough to lead in that which is good; and so many a good work that now lies undone would be done, if there were but a few active men to stir in it and put it forward. The novelty of the box had pleased the people's humour and won their gifts where mere exhortation might have failed, for an invention to please men's humour may sometimes bring them to their duty, and wisdom herein is profitable to direct. The giving was not extorted but delighted in; the reformation of the temple became, for a season, the joy of the nation.

The two witnesses do not divide, and together they set this bright scene as the high-water mark of Joash's early reign. Here is a king whose zeal has stirred a whole people, princes and commons alike, to open their hands with joy for the house of God; here is a reformation that has caught fire, the stalled collection now overflowing, the chest filled again and again until the work could be paid for and finished. Gill fixes the willing spirit of the givers; Henry the cheerfulness, the wisdom of the means, and the power of a few active leaders to carry a good cause. It is a moment of genuine gladness in the sacred story — the more poignant because the reader already knows how brief the springtime will be. The same king who now rejoices with his people over the mending of the temple will one day forsake it, and the same nation that pours its silver in with such delight will follow him into the groves and the idols when the aged priest who guided them both is gone.
11:
The verse follows the chest through its regular round — brought by the Levites to the king's officer, emptied, and set back in its place, "day by day" — and the witnesses attend to the procedure and to one telling change the chronicler has made in the older account. The reformed John Gill locates "the king's office" as the place where his appointed officer, or officers, met for this service, very probably in one of the chambers of the temple.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott renders the whole with care: "at the time when one used to bring the chest to the royal inspection by the hand of the Levites" — that is, whenever the chest seemed full, it was carried to the king's oversight, the chronicler being characteristically careful to record the participation of the Levites. Then "the king's scribe, or accountant, and the high priest's officer would come in and empty the chest, and the Levites would take it up and restore it to its place." Here Ellicott notes the divergence: the older record at Kings reads "the king's scribe and the high priest came up, and bound up and counted the money"; the chronicler has substituted "the high priest's officer" for "the high priest" himself. This, he judges, was done in the interest of the high priest's dignity — for in the chronicler's own day the high priesthood was invested with all the greater majesty in that the monarchy was a thing of the distant past, and it would not do to have so exalted a personage stooping to empty a collection-box. The phrase "day by day," he adds, means simply time after time, as often as the chest was full.

The two witnesses do not divide. Gill fixes the place of the reckoning; Ellicott the mechanics of the emptying, the Levites' share in it, and the small but revealing retouch by which a later age guarded the honour of its high priest. Between them they show the collection running now with orderly regularity — a chest filled, borne up, counted before scribe and priestly officer, and returned to its post at the gate to fill again — the reformation no longer stalled but humming along its appointed course. And in Ellicott's observation about the substituted "officer" the reader catches a glimpse of the chronicler at his work, transcribing the ancient annals yet shaping them, ever so slightly, to the reverence of his own generation, for whom the priesthood had become the abiding centre of a nation that had lost its kings.
12:
The money now flows out to the workmen — "the king and Jehoiada gave it to such as did the work of the service of the house of the LORD, and hired masons and carpenters, and workers in iron and brass, to mend the house" — and the witnesses attend to the labourers, the overseers, and the faithfulness that marked the whole business. The reformed John Gill explains that the king and priest gave the money to those who were overseers of the work, that they might pay the several artificers with it.

The grammatical-historical witnesses fix the grammar and the trades. Keil and Delitzsch gather the sense of the passage, and Charles Ellicott renders "to such as did the work" as "to the doer" — a word he takes in a collective sense, meaning those who had charge of the building, the Levitical inspectors of works, comparing the "doers of the work who were charged with the house of the LORD" at 2 Kings 12:11. "And hired" he reads as a continuous action: they were, from time to time, hiring masons and carpenters, as at 1 Chronicles 22:15; and "to mend" is "to repair," the same word as at v.4. The chronicler, he notes, has considerably abridged the fuller description of the workmen given in the older account.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry lifts the whole transaction into a lesson on fidelity. The king and Jehoiada faithfully paid the money to the workmen, he observes, and the workmen faithfully did the work; and faithfulness, he says, is the greatest praise, and will be the greatest comfort, of those who are entrusted with public treasure or employed in public business. It is a quiet commendation of honest stewardship on every hand — rulers who neither embezzled nor withheld, labourers who earned their wages by real toil — a chain of trust running from the throne to the mason's chisel. The witnesses do not divide. Gill fixes the flow of the money through the overseers; Keil and Ellicott the trades employed and the chronicler's abridgement of his source; Henry the faithfulness that made the enterprise prosper. Between them they show the restoration in full and orderly swing — silver counted at the chest, passed to trusty overseers, laid out in the wages of masons and carpenters and smiths, and turned into the mended stone and timber of the house of God. It is public religion at its best: a good work generously funded, honestly administered, and diligently done, every hand in the chain answerable and every hand faithful — the very picture of what a reformation ought to be, and the bright foil to the treachery that will darken the chapter's close.
13:
The work reaches its completion — "so the workmen wrought, and the work was perfected by them, and they set the house of God in his state, and strengthened it" — and the witnesses dwell on a vivid Hebrew metaphor and the restoration it describes. The reformed John Gill lists the labourers whose joint toil brought the house back: the masons, the carpenters, the blacksmiths, and the brasiers, each trade completing its part.

The grammatical-historical witnesses expound the figure. Keil and Delitzsch render the clause "there was a band laid upon the work" — a symbolical expression, they explain, for the furthering and restoration of the house of God, the same idiom that recurs at Nehemiah 4:1 and in the prophet Jeremiah. Charles Ellicott unfolds the same curious metaphor: "a bandage was applied to the work by their hand," a figure of healing used again of the walls of Jerusalem at Nehemiah 4, and by Jeremiah of the nation's restoration at Jeremiah 8:22 and Jeremiah 30:17. The battered temple is treated like a wounded body over which the physician binds his dressing — the breaches bandaged, the fabric knit together and made whole. "They set the house of God in his state," Ellicott adds, is better "they made the house of God to stand according to the measure thereof," that is, in its original proportions, restored to the very dimensions of its first design, the word being that used of exact measure at Exodus 30:32.

The two grammatical-historical voices note further that this verse has no counterpart in the older account; the chronicler alone records the perfecting of the work "before the king and Jehoiada," a phrase he favours. The witnesses do not divide. Gill names the trades; Keil and Ellicott expound the metaphor of the bandage and the restoration to the ancient measure. Between them they show the labour of the reign crowned at last — the house of God, so long defaced by Athaliah's brood, now healed of its wounds and standing again in its first proportions, sound and strengthened. It is the summit of Joash's good years, the visible monument of what a king and a priest, working together in faith, could accomplish; and the reader is meant to hold the image fast — the temple whole and firm again — for it is against this restored and shining house that the coming apostasy will be measured, when the very court now so carefully mended becomes the scene of a prophet's murder.
14:
The surplus of the collection is turned to holy use, and the reign's bright chapter closes with continual worship — "they made vessels for the house of the LORD... and they offered burnt offerings continually all the days of Jehoiada." The reformed John Gill notes simply that this followed the finishing of all the necessary repairs. The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley explains why new vessels were needed at all: Athaliah and her sons had carried the old ones away, as the earlier charge at v.7 declared, so that the sanctuary had to be re-furnished from the money left over.

The grammatical-historical witnesses fix the detail. Keil and Delitzsch explain that of the remainder the king caused vessels to be made for the house of Jahve — vessels of the service, according to Numbers 4:12, and vessels for the offering of burnt-offering, that is altar-vessels, together with bowls and other vessels of gold and silver; and they read the closing clause forward, that king and people offered burnt-offering continually so long as Jehoiada lived. Charles Ellicott takes "spoons" to mean cups or bowls, the kappoth of Exodus 25:29, and grapples with an apparent contradiction: the older record at 2 Kings 12:13-14 seems to say that no such vessels of gold and silver were made from the money brought into the house. The solution, Ellicott proposes, lies in the different vantage of the two writers — the author of Kings is telling what was done with the money so long as the repairs were in progress, when nothing was spent on ornament; the chronicler is accounting for the surplus after the restoration was complete, from which the vessels were at last supplied.

Ellicott presses the last clause: "they were offering" means they offered habitually, as a matter of regular observance, so that the legal ritual was duly carried out in the temple as long as the influence of Jehoiada was paramount — a remark, he notes, peculiar to the later historian. And there the qualifier tolls again, as at v.2: the sacrifices ascended continually, but only "all the days of Jehoiada." The witnesses do not divide. Gill and Wesley fix the occasion and the need for new vessels; Keil catalogues them; Ellicott harmonizes the seeming clash with Kings and marks the ominous time-limit. Between them they bring the reign's first act to its close on a note of full and faithful worship — a mended house, a re-furnished altar, the smoke of continual offering rising to heaven — and quietly warn, by that recurring "while Jehoiada lived," that all this piety hangs upon one aged life now drawing to its end.
15:
The chapter turns on a grave — "Jehoiada waxed old, and was full of days when he died; an hundred and thirty years old was he" — and the witnesses gather to honour the man and to mark the hinge his death becomes. The reformed John Gill notes only that he was a very old man, a rare instance in an age when few reached such years. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch weigh what the kingdom owed him: he had saved the life and throne of Joash, preserved to the realm the royal house of David to which the promises belonged, and put an end to the idolatry that Joram's marriage had transplanted into Judah, restoring the worship of the LORD; for all this he was honoured at his death, his body laid in the city of David among the kings, "for he had done good in Israel, and toward God, and toward his house."

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry and the wesleyan-arminian John Wesley dwell on the great age and the honour paid it. By his hundred and thirty years, they reckon, Jehoiada must have been born in Solomon's time and have lived through six entire reigns before this; they buried him among the kings with this honourable encomium — perhaps inscribed upon his gravestone — that he had done good in Israel, Judah being called Israel because, the other tribes having revolted from God, they only were Israelites indeed. But both draw the same sombre corollary: the little religion that Joash had was all buried in Jehoiada's grave, and see, Wesley cries, how great a judgment to any prince or people is the death of holy and useful men.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott attends to the language and the number. "Full of days" he renders "satisfied with days," a verb used only here and at 1 Chronicles 23:1, the older idiom being the adjectival "full of days" of Genesis 25:8. On the hundred and thirty years he is candid: modern physiology, he notes, reckons a far shorter span the ordinary limit of human life, and while such an age is not impossible under favourable conditions, an error of transcription in the text is also not impossible. The witnesses do not divide. Gill marks the rarity of the age; Keil the debt the kingdom owed the priest; Henry and Wesley the buried encomium and the buried religion; Ellicott the philology and the possible textual doubt. Between them they lay to rest the one man whose faith had upheld the reign, and prepare the reader for the swift collapse the next verses record — for when the prop is gone, the wall that leaned on it falls.
16:
The burial itself becomes a verdict — "they buried him in the city of David among the kings, because he had done good in Israel, both toward God, and toward his house" — and the witnesses read the singular honour paid to a priest laid among sovereigns. The reformed John Gill sees it as a fitting tribute to the preserver of the king and of the kingdom, one who was moreover, by marriage, uncle to the reigning king. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke presses the point further: Jehoiada had in fact been king in Judah, for the weak Joash was always under his tutelage, and the priest governed the state in the young king's name; his burial among the kings is a plain proof of the high estimation in which the people held him.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch confirm the ground of the honour — he was laid among the kings because he had done good in Israel, toward God and toward his house, the temple — and read the verse as the threshold of the reversal, for hard upon this burial the princes of Judah will come and make obeisance to the king. Charles Ellicott adds the reasons for so exceptional a distinction: not the good he had done only, but also, perhaps, his having been regent for so many years and his connection by marriage with the royal house, as at 2 Chronicles 22:11. The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley glosses the word "Israel," insisting that Judah is here meant, an eminent part of Israel and the only part that then owned God or was owned by God as his Israel — a name Scripture often appropriates to the faithful remnant.

The witnesses do not divide. Gill and Clarke exalt the honour as due to one who had been the true ruler and saviour of the realm; Keil and Ellicott ground it in his goodness, his long regency, and his royal kinship; Wesley fixes the sense of the name. Between them they set up a deliberate contrast that the chapter will not let the reader forget. Here a priest is buried among kings for the good he did; at the chapter's close a king will be buried apart from the kings for the evil he did, denied the royal tombs that Jehoiada, though no king by blood, was thought worthy to share. The one who served God faithfully to a hundred and thirty years lies in honour among the sovereigns of Judah; the one born to the throne will lie in disgrace outside their sepulchres. The burial of Jehoiada is thus both a tribute and a prophecy, measuring in advance the worth of the two men by the company each keeps in death.
17:
No sooner is the old priest in his grave than the reign changes colour — "after the death of Jehoiada came the princes of Judah, and made obeisance to the king; then the king hearkened unto them" — and the witnesses read the courtly bow as the opening of a fatal seduction. The reformed John Gill judges that these princes had long been secretly inclined to idolatry but durst not discover it during Jehoiada's life, his influence at court being too great to counterwork; now, with him dead, they come to press their suit. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott explains that they made obeisance as men asking a boon, their petition evident from what follows at v.18: they sought the royal sanction for the idolatrous forms of worship after which they hankered, and the king hearkened to them, just as the young Rehoboam had hearkened to the flattering counsel of his youthful courtiers at 2 Chronicles 10:8.

The wesleyan-arminian witnesses expose the manner and the motive. Adam Clarke gives the Targum's blunt paraphrase — the great men came and adored King Joash, and seduced him, and then the king received from them their idols. John Wesley reads the request they carried under their obeisance: that they might not be confined to troublesome journeys to Jerusalem but might have the liberty their forefathers had enjoyed of worshipping in the high places; and this liberty once obtained, they knew they could worship idols without disturbance, which was the very thing they aimed at — for the prevention of such abuses God had bound all to worship him in one place.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry draws the psychology of the fall. Bad counsellors got about the king and wheedled him, congratulating him on the death of his old tutor as his release from grave lessons and restraints, telling him he was priest-ridden no longer and might now do as he pleased; and, Henry marvels, it was the princes of Judah themselves who were so industrious to debauch him. They made obeisance, flattering him into an opinion of his own absolute power, promising to stand by him in making his royal will pass for law; and he hearkened, for their discourse pleased him better than Jehoiada's plain dealing ever had. Those who incline to the counsel of the ungodly, Henry warns, will never want ungodly counsellors. The witnesses do not divide. Gill uncovers the long-hidden bent of the princes; Ellicott and Wesley the petition for the high places that masked a hunger for idols; Clarke the seduction; Henry the flattery that undid a weak man the moment his prop was gone. Between them they show how swiftly a borrowed goodness collapses — the king who had rejoiced over the temple now bowed to by men who mean to draw him from it, and bending at the first push.
18:
The seduction bears its bitter fruit — "they left the house of the LORD God of their fathers, and served groves and idols; and wrath came upon Judah and Jerusalem for this their trespass" — and the witnesses read the apostasy and the anger it kindled. The reformed John Gill states it plainly: they came no more to the temple at Jerusalem but forsook its worship and service altogether. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott sharpens the object of their new devotion — they served "the Asherim and the idols" — and reads the wrath that came as the divine displeasure of Numbers 1:53, which in this case took the concrete form of a Syrian invasion, the sin of the nobles, allowed and perhaps imitated by the king, involving the whole nation in its penal consequences. Keil and Delitzsch name the same judgment: the wrath, they say, is that wrathful visitation of the LORD spoken of at 2 Chronicles 29:8, namely the invasion of the land by Hazael the Syrian.

The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley marvels at the sheer inconstancy of it: the king and princes who but a little while ago had so zealously repaired the temple now forsook the temple — so inconstant a thing is man, and so little confidence is to be put in him. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry unfolds the whole reversal. The princes, he supposes, had a request they durst not offer while Jehoiada lived — that they might set up again the groves and idols thrown down at the beginning of the reign, hating to be confined to the dull, old-fashioned service of the temple; and the king not only gave them leave but joined them in it. Those who a little while ago were repairing the temple now forsook it; those who had pulled down groves and idols now themselves served them. So inconstant a thing is man, Henry echoes, and so little is he to be trusted when the restraints of grace and good company are removed.

The witnesses do not divide. Gill fixes the plain fact of the desertion; Ellicott and Keil name the wrath and the Syrian rod it would wield; Wesley and Henry lament the inconstancy of men who could swing so far and so fast from reformation to idolatry. Between them they show the tragedy of a merely external religion laid bare: the moment the strong hand of Jehoiada was withdrawn, the temple he had restored stood empty of its king and princes, the groves he had felled rose again, and the anger of God — so long held off by one man's faith — was kindled against Judah and Jerusalem. The reformation of a reign proved to be the reformation of a single life; and now that life was gone.
19:
Even in the nation's revolt God does not at once strike but sends messengers — "yet he sent prophets to them, to bring them again unto the LORD; and they testified against them, but they would not give ear" — and the witnesses read the verse as a monument to divine patience. The reformed John Gill dwells on the clemency: God sent prophets to reprove them for their sin, to warn them of their danger, to exhort them to their duty, and so to endeavour their restoration and recovery to the obedience and worship of God — all this in his goodness and condescension before he executed his wrath upon them. Mercy pleads before judgment falls.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott fixes the force of the words. "Yet" is simply "and"; "to them" is better "among them"; and "they testified against them" means that the prophets solemnly besought and exhorted them in the name of God, the same weighty verb of adjuration that meets us at 2 Kings 17:13, where the LORD testifies against Israel and Judah by all the prophets. The closing clause, "but they would not give ear," Ellicott reads as the flat record of a settled refusal — the word came, and they simply would not hear it.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry expounds the whole as the work and the frustration of the prophetic ministry. It is the office of ministers, he says, to bring people not to themselves but to God — to bring back to him those who have gone a-whoring from him; and in the most degenerate times God left not himself without witness, sending prophets to convince and instruct even a people who had dealt so disingenuously with him, and assuring them that they should yet find favour if they would but return, for he would rather that sinners should turn and live than go on and die, and those who perish shall be left inexcusable. The prophets did their part, Henry allows: they testified against them faithfully; but few or none received their testimony, for the people were so strangely wedded to their idols that no reproofs nor warnings nor any of the various methods the prophets used could reclaim them. The witnesses do not divide. Gill exalts the mercy of the warning; Ellicott fixes the solemn testimony and the deaf refusal; Henry unfolds the ministry that pleaded in vain. Between them they show a God slow to anger even against apostates, stretching out his hand all the day long to a disobedient and gainsaying people — and a people so hardened that they left the messengers of grace no answer but a stopped ear, and so ripened themselves, warning by rejected warning, for the stroke that patience had long delayed.
20:
Among the prophets sent, one stands out — "the Spirit of God came upon Zechariah the son of Jehoiada the priest, who stood above the people, and said, Why transgress ye the commandments of the LORD, that ye cannot prosper? because ye have forsaken the LORD, he hath also forsaken you." The reformed John Gill glosses the descent of the Spirit as the spirit of prophecy, the Targum's phrase, that moved and influenced Zechariah to speak. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott renders it more vividly — the Spirit "clothed" or invested him, the same figure as at 1 Chronicles 12:18 — and fixes the identity: "the priest" is the epithet of Jehoiada, not of Zechariah, so that this is the son of the very man who had saved and reared the king. He pictures the prophet standing above the people, probably on the steps of the inner court, facing the crowd gathered in the outer; and the reciprocal sentence, "because ye have forsaken the LORD, he hath forsaken you," he sets beside the like words of Azariah and of Shemaiah at 2 Chronicles 15:2 and 2 Chronicles 12:5.

The wesleyan-arminian witnesses add colour from the tradition. Adam Clarke gives the Targum's fuller scene: when Zechariah saw the transgression of the king and people, burning incense to an idol in the sanctuary of the LORD on the day of expiation, and preventing the priests from offering the daily services written in the law of Moses, he stood above the people and spoke. John Wesley pictures the people assembled in the temple court, which they had not quite forsaken, when Zechariah stood up in one of the raised places among the priests and plainly told them their sin and the consequence of it.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry expounds the message itself. Zechariah, filled with the spirit of prophecy, told the people of their sin plainly but without any provoking language, reminding them only of what was written in the law: the precept they broke, in serving groves and idols, and the penalty they incurred, that they could not prosper in this evil way. "Because you have forsaken the Lord, he hath forsaken you," Henry glosses from Deuteronomy 31:16-17 — never expect to do ill and fare well; and this, he says, is the work of ministers, by the word of God to expose the sin of men and expound the providences of God. The witnesses do not divide. Gill and Ellicott fix the Spirit's clothing and the prophet's parentage; Clarke and Wesley the scene and its solemn day; Henry the plain, unprovoking, scriptural charge. Between them they set the son of Joash's benefactor before the apostate throng, speaking not his own word but God's — the last warning before the blood.
21:
The warning is answered with murder — "they conspired against him, and stoned him with stones at the commandment of the king, in the court of the house of the LORD" — and the witnesses recoil from a crime they rank among the blackest in all the history of the kings. The reformed John Gill notes that they consulted together to take away his life and procured the king's order to do it. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke can scarcely contain his horror: what a wretched and contemptible man was this, who could imbrue his hands in the blood of a prophet of God, and the son of the very man who had saved him from being murdered and raised him to the throne; can even kings forget benefits so? But when a man falls from God, Clarke says, the devil enters into him, and then he is capable of every species of cruelty.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott supplies the legal and prophetic frame. Stoning was the appointed penalty of idolatry, at Deuteronomy 17:2-5 and Leviticus 20:2 — so the apostates turned the law's own sanction against the man who reproved their apostasy. Zechariah's words, Ellicott suggests, had probably been represented to Joash as treasonable, the Syrian invasion perhaps already threatening, so that his prophecy could be branded as disloyal, much as Jeremiah's would be at Jeremiah 32:1-5 and as Naboth was falsely condemned at 1 Kings 21:8-13. And there is little doubt, he adds, that our Lord's own reference to "Zacharias son of Barachias, whom ye slew between the temple and the altar," at Matthew 23:35 and Luke 11:51, points to this very murder, the altar standing in the court before the temple.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry and the wesleyan-arminian John Wesley heap up the aggravations. They stoned him immediately, in a popular tumult, without even the colour of law; and the Jews reckon seven transgressions bound up in the one deed, for they killed a priest, a prophet, and a judge, shed innocent blood, and polluted the court of the temple, the sabbath, and the day of expiation, on which tradition says it fell. The person was sacred, Henry adds, the place sacred — the inner court between the porch and the altar — and the message sacred, known to come from the Spirit of prophecy; yet a king in covenant with God commanded the murder of one whom it was his very office to protect. The witnesses do not divide. Gill fixes the conspiracy and the royal warrant; Clarke the monstrous ingratitude; Ellicott the perverted law, the trumped-up treason, and the New Testament seal upon the crime; Henry and Wesley its manifold sacrilege. Between them they render the reign's nadir — a prophet stoned in God's own courtyard at the word of the king his father had crowned.
22:
The historian pauses to name the sin by its true name — ingratitude — and to record the martyr's dying word. "Joash the king remembered not the kindness which Jehoiada his father had done to him, but slew his son; and when he died, he said, The LORD look upon it, and require it." The reformed John Gill spells out the kindness forgotten: Jehoiada had preserved Joash in his infancy and nourished him, had set him on the throne, and had aided him with his counsel — and all this the king repaid with the blood of the benefactor's son. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch mark the same forgetting and read the dying cry as the pivot on which the chapter turns to judgment, for the punishment comes hard upon it.

Over that cry the witnesses gather with care. Charles Ellicott renders it "Jehovah behold, and avenge" — literally, seek vengeance for the crime, as at Genesis 9:5 and Psalms 10:4 — and observes that this dying imprecation is in harmony with the spirit of the older dispensation, which exacted blood for blood; he sets it in deliberate contrast with the prayer of the first Christian martyr, who cried rather that his enemies' sin be not laid to their charge, at Acts 7:60. Yet the prayer was also a prophecy, Ellicott adds, destined to speedy fulfilment. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry insists that it came not from a spirit of revenge but from a spirit of prophecy: "he will require it"; it would be the continual cry of the shed blood, as Abel's blood cried against Cain, and Christ himself makes the persecutors of the gospel answerable for the blood of this Zechariah at Matthew 23:35, so that it joins the cry of the souls under the altar at Revelation 6:10. The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley reads it much the same, that the LORD will make inquisition for innocent blood and require satisfaction; and Adam Clarke notes grimly how swiftly the requiring came — before the year was out the Syrians destroyed the princes, and the king was murdered in his bed.

So the witnesses circle a real nuance without quite dividing. Ellicott hears in the words the sterner justice of the old covenant, blood for blood, a note the gospel would soften; Henry and Wesley soften it themselves, reading not personal vengeance but prophetic certainty that God would avenge. What none doubts is the depth of the ingratitude the verse indicts — call a man ungrateful, Henry says, and you can call him no worse — nor the swiftness of the recompense the dying prophet foresaw.
23:
The requiring falls at once — "at the end of the year the host of Syria came up against him, and came to Judah and Jerusalem, and destroyed all the princes of the people, and sent all their spoil to the king of Damascus." The reformed John Gill marks the terrible promptness: it was at the end of the year after Zechariah's death, so soon did his prophecy have its accomplishment. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry reads the invasion as bare judgment: God's people, while they kept close to him, had often conquered against far greater numbers, but now, because they had forsaken the LORD God of their fathers, they were routed by a small Syrian force — for their God had not only departed from them but turned to be their enemy and fought against them, the Syrians serving unwittingly as the instrument in his hand.

The grammatical-historical witnesses fix the manoeuvre. Keil and Delitzsch date it "at the revolution of a year," scarcely a year after the murder, when a Syrian army invaded Judah and advanced upon Jerusalem; the chronicler, they note, brings forward only those parts of the campaign that show how God punished Joash for his defection. Charles Ellicott reads the verse against the fuller account at 2 Kings 12:17 and infers that a small detachment of the besieging army was sent against Jerusalem: the princes of Judah, at the head of a large force, met the invaders in the field, but the Syrians routed them and "destroyed all the princes of the people from among the people," making it their special aim to cut off the leaders of the host. Thus the apostate princes — the very men who at v.17 had seduced the king — were overtaken by the prophetic doom, and the spoil was sent to Hazael, still with the main body of his troops.

The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley draws the same moral: so soon did God hear the cry of his holy prophet's blood and revenge it; and the princes were struck first, that it might appear they were singled out by God for destruction as the first beginners of the general apostasy. The witnesses do not divide. Gill and Wesley mark the swiftness of the vengeance; Henry the divine hand behind the defeat; Keil and Ellicott the strategy by which a small force cut down the ringleaders. Between them they show the dying imprecation answered to the letter — the princes who had led the king astray destroyed within the year, the treasures carried off to Damascus, and a whole nation learning that the blood shed in the temple court had a swift and certain Avenger.
24:
The disproportion of the defeat is itself the sermon — "the army of the Syrians came with a small company of men, and the LORD delivered a very great host into their hand, because they had forsaken the LORD God of their fathers; so they executed judgment against Joash." The reformed John Gill notes only that the Syrian force consisted but of few. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry seizes the point: an inconsiderable handful of Syrians routed a very great host of Israelites, because they had forsaken the LORD God of their fathers, so that they were not merely put on a level with their enemies but opposed them at the utmost disadvantage — the Syrians being employed, all unknowing, as the instruments in God's hand to execute his judgments, as the Assyrian rod would be at Isaiah 10:6-7, and as one might chase a thousand only when their Rock had sold them, at Deuteronomy 32:30.

The grammatical-historical witnesses fix the wording and the sequel. Keil and Delitzsch read the verse as showing how the LORD gave a great host into the hand of a few because they had forsaken him, and so executed judgment upon Joash. Charles Ellicott renders it "for with fewness of men had the host of Syria come, and Jehovah had given into their hand a host in exceeding abundance," a phrase found only here; and he supplies from the parallel what the chronicler omits — that Hazael had meant to march on Jerusalem in person, but that Joash bribed his forbearance with a present of the treasures of the temple and the palace, as recorded at 2 Kings 12:18. The expression "they executed judgment against Joash," Ellicott observes, is one always used of divine requital, as at Exodus 12:12; the whole narrative regards the Syrian invasion from a prophetic and religious point of view, and therefore, while it omits certain military details given in Kings, it is careful to mention just those facts that most vividly point its moral — the destruction of the idolatrous princes, and the rout of a great host by a small company.

The witnesses do not divide. Gill and Henry press the theology of the few overcoming the many; Keil and Ellicott the exact wording of the requital and the bribe by which Joash bought off the invader with the very treasures of the house he had once repaired. Between them they show the deepest irony of the judgment: the king who had gathered a nation's silver to mend the temple now strips that temple to save his own skin, and the God who had given him victory in his faithful years now gives a great army into the hand of a few — for the arithmetic of battle is nothing when the LORD has become a people's foe.
25:
The judgment closes in upon the king himself — "when they were departed from him, for they left him in great diseases, his own servants conspired against him for the blood of the sons of Jehoiada the priest, and slew him on his bed." The reformed John Gill notes only that the Syrians withdrew when they had got what spoil they could. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott corrects and fills in the scene: the Syrians retired instead of besieging Jerusalem, and "left him in great diseases" — a rare word meaning pains or sufferings, close kin to the term used of Jehoram's mortal sickness at 2 Chronicles 21:19; whether the calamity brought on the sickness, or the invasion found him already prostrate and unable to take the field in person, the king was left broken. His own servants then conspired against him, as at 2 Kings 12:20, and slew him on his bed, much as Ishbosheth had been slain at 2 Samuel 4:5.

Over the phrase "the blood of the sons of Jehoiada" the witnesses divide. The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley takes the plural at face value: by this it seems Joash slew not only Zechariah but his brothers also, and perhaps the assassins meant to avenge that innocent blood — though what they intended, God intended in permitting it. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry reads it the same way, that the king slew others of Jehoiada's sons besides Zechariah, and that those who drink the blood of the saints shall have their own blood given them to drink. Ellicott, more cautious, notes that the Septuagint and Vulgate read "son," meaning Zechariah alone, and judges the plural either a transcriber's slip or, more probably, a rhetorical form as at 2 Chronicles 28:16 — the writer meaning not that revenge for a whole family was the assassins' motive, but that their deed was a judgment upon the king for that one crime.

On the burial all agree, and Henry sharpens it: the people would not bury him in the sepulchres of the kings, as Ellicott notes they had likewise refused the wicked Jehoram at 2 Chronicles 21:20; he had stained his honour, and, in Henry's phrase from the Psalm, was not to be written with the righteous, at Psalms 69:28. The witnesses do not finally divide. Gill and Ellicott fix the disease and the murder in the bed; Wesley and Henry read a wider slaughter of Jehoiada's house avenged; Ellicott weighs the plural as rhetoric. Between them they show the measure filled — the murderer of a prophet murdered in his sickbed, and denied at last the royal grave.
26:
The historian names the assassins, and notes a detail the older record omits — their foreign mothers. "These are they that conspired against him: Zabad the son of Shimeath an Ammonitess, and Jehozabad the son of Shimrith a Moabitess." The reformed John Gill observes that the first is called Jozachar, the son of Shimeath, in the parallel at Kings. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott works through the variants: "Jozachar" of 2 Kings 12:21 is probably the right form, "Zabad" being an easy corruption of "Zachar"; and "Shomer" in Kings should likely be Shemer, of which Shimri and Shimrith may be by-forms. The maternal names, he insists against Reuss, are not substituted for the fathers' but added to them, and — most importantly — they indicate the use of another source than the canonical book of Kings, the same distinct source that gave the chronicler his strikingly original account of the death of Zechariah.

Over the meaning of those foreign names the witnesses part. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry finds in them a providential irony: it is observable, he says, that the mothers of both were foreigners, one an Ammonitess and the other a Moabitess; the idolatrous kings countenanced the very marriages the law had prohibited to prevent idolatry, and see how they resulted in their own destruction. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke turns it to a warning of statecraft: these two were certainly not Jews but aliens, probably officers of the king's chamber with the easiest access to his person; and it has ever been the folly of kings to keep foreigners as their most confidential servants, who have often been the causes of murders and treacheries. But Ellicott will have none of such moralizing when it is pressed too far: the critic Thenius, he notes, even claims to know why the chronicler added the epithets "Ammonitess" and "Moabitess" — to show that the idolatry into which Joash lapsed was avenged by two sons of idolatrous wives — and this, Ellicott retorts, is "fancy determined by prejudice."

So the witnesses genuinely differ over the significance of the detail. Henry and Clarke read the foreign parentage as charged with meaning — the recoil of forbidden marriages, the peril of alien servants; Ellicott takes it as no moral emblem at all but simply a mark of the chronicler's fuller and independent source. Gill fixes the textual variant; Ellicott the philology and the source-critical point; Henry and Clarke the providential and political lessons. Between them they close the account of the conspirators with both a caution and a corrective — the one side hearing judgment in the assassins' very ancestry, the other warning against reading more into it than the sober historian meant.
27:
The reign is signed off with the customary formula, though a single word in it puzzles the witnesses — "now concerning his sons, and the greatness of the burdens laid upon him, and the repairing of the house of God, behold, they are written in the story of the book of the kings. And Amaziah his son reigned in his stead." The reformed John Gill notes only that the reference to "his sons" concerns how many they were and what their names.

The crux is the word rendered "burdens." The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke takes it of the heavy tribute the Syrians laid upon Joash, though he allows some understand rather the vast sums amassed for the repairs of the temple. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott shows why the word is uncertain: massa' is common in the sense of a threatening prophecy, as at Isaiah 13:1 and Habakkuk 1:1, so that "the multitude of oracles upon him" may be meant — the prophets sent to warn him at v.19, the word used collectively; yet another possible rendering is "the greatness of the tribute laid upon him" by Hazael, as the same word bears the sense of tribute at 2 Chronicles 17:11. The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley cuts to the sense he prefers: the "burdens" are the great judgments of God upon Joash, both by the Syrians and by his sore diseases.

On the source the two philologists agree. Clarke explains that "the story" is the midrash, the commentary of the book of Kings, one of those works now lost save for the extracts preserved in Kings, Chronicles, and Ezra — abridgments, he reflects, being often the very cause of the neglect and final destruction of the fuller originals. Ellicott too identifies it as the Midrash of the book of the kings, the distinct source that had furnished the chronicler his fuller matter throughout the chapter. So the witnesses close the reign together, differing only over the shade of one word. Gill fixes the reference to the sons; Clarke and Wesley read the "burdens" as the tribute and the judgments that crushed the apostate king; Ellicott weighs whether they were prophetic oracles or Syrian tribute, and names the vanished Midrash from which the record came. Between them they lay Joash to rest as the chapter's whole argument requires — a king who began by repairing the house of God and ended crushed under burdens of oracle and tribute and disease alike, his throne passing to Amaziah his son, and his story consigned to a book that time would not preserve.
